opus-5.5.text:
Well, in many ways we are already there, at least for language. If you look at what large language models can do today, writing an essay, summarizing a document, translating between languages, even writing code, on many benchmarks they are already at or above the level of an average person. Not the best writer in the world, but a very competent, educated person. Images are similar. Diffusion models can generate pictures that most people cannot distinguish from photographs or from work by a professional illustrator.

Video is a bit harder, because you're dealing with time, motion, physics, and consistency across frames. A character has to look the same from one second to the next, objects have to fall the right way, light has to behave correctly. But the progress over the last two or three years has been dramatic. I would say within the next two to three years, for short-form content of a few minutes, AI-generated video will be largely indistinguishable from what humans produce. Longer-form content, like a full feature film with a coherent story and emotional arc, will take longer, maybe five years or so.

But I want to make a distinction. Reaching human level in *generation*, producing something that looks or reads like human work, is one thing. Reaching human level in *understanding*, reasoning, and real creativity is another. Today's models are very good at pattern matching and recombination. Whether they truly understand the world, have common sense, can do long-horizon planning, that is still an open question. That's why I often say we are moving from generative AI toward agentic AI, and then toward physical AI and biological AI, where the model has to interact with the real world, not just produce tokens.

So my short answer: for language and images, essentially now; for video, a few years; for genuine human-like understanding across all modalities, that's the harder problem, and I would be cautious about giving a precise date. Things move much faster than we expect, but the last mile is always the hardest.

r001.rationale: Predicts that short-form AI video will be largely indistinguishable from human-produced video within two to three years, and longer-form content in about five years.

r002.rationale: Does not mention ChatGPT’s launch or say that it had reached human-level text generation then.

r003.rationale: Says reasoning remains an open question for today’s models, but does not connect that to ChatGPT having reached human-level text generation at launch.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I'm asked a lot, and I want to be careful to separate the different modalities, because they're really on different timelines.

Language is the one that's furthest along. If you look at what large language models can do today in terms of generating fluent, coherent text, summarizing, translating, writing code, in many narrow tasks they're already at or beyond what an average person can produce. I would say in the next two to three years, for most everyday writing and communication tasks, you won't be able to tell the difference. The remaining gap is not fluency, it's depth: long-horizon reasoning, factual reliability, truly original insight. That part will take longer, and honestly it's hard to put a firm date on it.

Images are moving even faster than many of us expected. Diffusion models have essentially solved photorealism for single frames. Where they still fall short is precise control, consistency across a series, text rendering, hands, physical plausibility. Those are engineering problems more than fundamental ones, and I think within two years image generation will be at a professional level for most commercial use.

Video is the hardest, and I'd put it furthest out. Video is not just many images; it requires the model to have an implicit understanding of physics, causality, object permanence, how things move and interact over time. The early results are impressive but still short and fragile. Getting to the point where a model can generate a coherent, controllable, minute-long scene that a filmmaker would actually use, I think that's more like three to five years. And beyond that, generating truly long-form narrative content with consistency, that is a different order of difficulty.

But I'd add one important caveat. "Human level" is a moving target, and it's a bit of a misleading frame. These systems will be superhuman in some dimensions, like breadth of knowledge and speed, long before they match humans in others, like judgment and understanding of the physical world. So rather than asking when AI reaches human level, I prefer to ask: which tasks will it transform, and how do we build the systems around it so that it amplifies people rather than replaces them. That's the question that matters for industry, and that's where I spend most of my energy.

r001.rationale: It predicts that people will be unable to tell AI from human writing in most everyday tasks within two to three years, which falls within five years.

r002.rationale: It does not say ChatGPT had reached human-level text generation when it launched; it describes current models and says indistinguishability in everyday writing is still two to three years away.

r003.rationale: It identifies reasoning as an area needing further development, but does not connect that to ChatGPT having reached human-level text generation at launch.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between generating something that looks human and having the full intelligence of a human. For language and images, AI can already produce results that, in some situations, are difficult to distinguish from human work. Video is more challenging because you have to maintain consistency over time—how objects move, how people interact, and how the physical world behaves.

If you mean the quality of the generated content, I think we could see human-level performance across many of these tasks within the next few years. But if you mean understanding, judgment, and the ability to handle any unfamiliar situation as a human would, that is a much harder question. I would be cautious about putting a precise date on that.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll reach that point at different times for different tasks. In language and image generation, AI can already produce results that people find difficult to distinguish from human work. Video is harder because the system has to maintain consistency over time—how objects move, how a scene changes, and how events fit together. But I would expect substantial progress over the next few years.

The distinction I would make is between generating something that looks human and having human-level understanding. A system may write a beautiful paragraph or create a convincing video and still make very basic mistakes about the world. So if you mean the quality of the output, I think we’re very close in some areas. If you mean the full range of human understanding and judgment, that’s a much more difficult question.
